transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you into the clinic?

Well, my regular doctor thought I should come talk to someone. I guess it's mostly because I've been trying to get to the bottom of my father's death. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly, but... well, I work as a computer systems analyst. I analyze data for a living. 

Actually, just last Tuesday we had this massive server migration at work, and the vendor tried to claim the data transfer was complete. But I found a huge discrepancy in the logs. People are just so careless with their jobs these days, you know? My coworker, Dave, he didn't even bother to verify the checksums before clocking out for the weekend, so I was stuck at the office until 9 PM fixing his mess. I ended up completely missing my dinner reservations. It was supposed to be a date, actually. First one in months, and she just ghosted me after that. Can't say I blame her, I guess, the restaurant was really hard to get into, but... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, my dad's records. So, when I actually sit down and compare the timestamps on those hospital files, and I look at the missing attachments, plus the way certain community members completely avoid my questions when I ask them about that night... it’s just obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened.
During this time, have you ever heard any voices or sounds that other people around you couldn't hear?

No, I haven't heard anything like that. No voices or anything. I mean, my hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, I do wear these high-end noise-canceling headphones at work a lot because the constant hum from the HVAC near my desk drives me absolutely crazy. I got the new Sony ones, they're supposed to block out like 99% of background noise, but the Bluetooth connection constantly drops whenever someone uses the microwave in the breakroom. It's a 2.4 gigahertz interference issue. 

I tried explaining this to our office manager, Linda, so she would just buy a newer microwave with better shielding, but she looked at me like I was speaking a completely different language. People really just do not grasp basic radio frequency concepts, you know? It's frustrating when you're just trying to focus on some code or listen to a podcast and your audio keeps cutting out because someone wants to heat up their leftover fish. Which, by the way, is a terrible thing to do in a shared office. But... wait, sorry, what were you asking me? Oh, right, hearing things. Yeah, no, I don't hear anything that isn't actually there.
Have you noticed any times where you felt completely energized despite sleeping significantly less than usual?

No, I wouldn't say I've felt like that. I usually sleep about the same amount every night. I mean, unless I get stuck on a problem at work, of course. Sometimes I'll be up late staring at a script that just refuses to compile, and I swear, the syntax highlighting in my IDE starts blurring together. I actually just switched to a new dark theme because the contrast on the old one was giving me eye strain. It's called "Solarized Dark," I highly recommend it if you ever have to stare at text all day. 

My optometrist told me I needed to follow that 20-20-20 rule, you know, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, but who actually remembers to do that? I tried setting a timer on my phone, but the notification sound just startled me every time it went off. I ended up disabling it because it kept interrupting my flow state. Once you lose that focus, it takes like twenty-three minutes to get back into it. I read a study about that once. But, um... sorry, I lost my train of thought. Sleep, right? No, I don't get those bursts of energy without sleep. I definitely need my coffee in the morning if I haven't gotten my full seven hours.

Like my thoughts or actions are being controlled by someone else? No, definitely not. I'm always the one in the driver's seat. 

Though, speaking of controlling things, I actually do a lot of remote desktop takeovers at work. When a user messes up their machine, I have this administrative software where I can literally just take control of their mouse and keyboard right from my desk. It freaks them out sometimes. Just yesterday, the HR director—she somehow managed to change her display settings so everything was completely upside down and in high contrast mode. I have absolutely no idea how she managed to bypass the group policy to do that. Windows 11 has this weird quirk with the accessibility shortcuts, and I had to remote in and fix it while she was on the phone with me. She joked that her computer was possessed, but I had to explain to her that it was just a shortcut she probably accidentally hit with her elbow. 

People rest their elbows or books on their keyboards all the time, which is terrible for the mechanical switches, by the way. I use Cherry MX Brown switches on my own keyboard at home—they give you that really nice tactile bump without the loud, obnoxious click, you know? I can't stand the blue switches, they sound like a typewriter from the 1980s. But... wait, sorry, what were you asking me? Oh, right, if I felt controlled. Yeah, no. Nobody is controlling me or my thoughts. My mind is my own.
How long have you been looking into your father's death and noticing these issues with the records?

It's been about nine months now. It started right after he died, when I had to start sorting through all his personal records and going through his messages to close out his accounts. 

Which, let me tell you, closing accounts for a deceased relative is an absolute nightmare. The amount of paperwork and verification they want is ridiculous. I had to fax—yes, fax, in this day and age—a copy of the death certificate to his bank because they wouldn't accept a secure PDF upload. I mean, fax machines are inherently insecure! The data is sent completely unencrypted over analog phone lines, and anyone with a butt set could just tap the line at the demarc box and intercept it. It blows my mind that the financial sector still relies on a technology from the 1970s for "security." 

I actually tried to explain to the bank representative that I could set up an end-to-end encrypted file transfer using PGP keys, but she just kept repeating her script about company policy. It's like talking to a poorly programmed chatbot. I've actually been messing around with some open-source LLMs locally on my machine at home, just to see if I could train one to handle customer service calls better than these banks do. You need a ton of VRAM to run the decent models, though. I had to upgrade my GPU to a 4090, which was a pain to fit into my case because the heatsink on those things is massive. I had to completely reroute my liquid cooling tubes just to get the side panel to close. 

But... wait, sorry. You were asking about the timeline, right? Yeah, it's been about nine months since I started noticing all the discrepancies in his files.
Before your father passed away, did you generally find it difficult to trust other people?

No, I wouldn't say I had trust issues before. I mean, I'm a systems analyst, so my default state is healthy skepticism, but I didn't think people were actively out to get me or lying to me on a daily basis. 

Honestly, trusting people is a lot like trusting a new software update. You want to believe the patch notes when they say it fixes bugs and improves stability, but experience tells you to wait a week before deploying it to production just in case it breaks everything. Like last month, Microsoft pushed out an update that completely bricked the VPN client we use for our remote workers. It was a disaster. I had over fifty tickets in the queue before I even finished my first cup of coffee. I had to write a PowerShell script to automatically roll back the update on all the affected machines, which took me hours to test because you have to make sure you don't accidentally uninstall the wrong KB package. If you mess up the registry keys during a rollback, you can put the machine into an endless boot loop, and then you have to manually re-image the whole drive. 

I actually keep a bootable USB drive on my keychain with a lightweight Linux distro and a bunch of diagnostic tools just in case I need to do emergency data recovery. It's saved my neck more times than I can count. The drive itself is this really cool rugged metal one that's supposed to be waterproof up to 100 meters, not that I'm planning on doing any deep-sea diving with my IT equipment anytime soon. I did go snorkeling once in Hawaii, though. The coral reefs were amazing, but I got a terrible sunburn on my back because I forgot to reapply sunscreen. 

But, uh, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, trusting people. No, before all this stuff with my dad, I was pretty normal about trusting people. I didn't have any reason not to.
